what: The context builder decides exactly what goes into the model's prompt: which passages, in what order, with what labels, cut to fit a token budget.
like: Like packing a carry-on bag: limited space, so you pick the essentials, drop duplicates, and put what you need first on top.
why: More context is not better - the right few passages beat a stuffed window
Token budget controls cost and latency on every call
Stable ordering lets prompt caching reuse the expensive prefix

nodes.t: Order + label|best at start or end

steps.d: Candidates arrive already scored by retrieval and reranking. Packing is ranking plus truncation: take the best until the budget is spent.
Near-duplicate chunks (same page crawled twice, overlapping windows) waste tokens. Drop them and keep some variety across sources so one site does not crowd out the rest.
A small chunk is good for matching but thin for answering. Pull in its neighbours or parent section so the model sees the full thought.
Give each passage an id, title, URL and date (metadata). Models use the start and end of the context best, so put the strongest evidence there.
Count tokens for system prompt, tools, history, passages and room for the answer. Cut the lowest-ranked passages first, never the instructions.
Put unchanging parts first - tools, system prompt, shared documents - then the per-question parts. A stable prefix can be cached and reused cheaply.

choices.d: Reserve fixed shares for instructions, history, retrieved passages and the answer (max output). Retrieval gets what is left, not whatever it returns.
Fewer, better passages after reranking usually beat many. Tune top-k against answer quality and citation recall on your eval set, not by gut feel.
Small chunks for matching, then expand to neighbours or the parent section for reading. Bigger windows mean more context per hit and fewer hits.
Best evidence first (and optionally a strong one last), with stable sections at the very top so caching works. Avoid burying key facts in the middle.
Use compaction (summarise older turns) and clear stale tool results instead of letting history grow until the window overflows.

instead.why: Better candidates upstream make packing easier
Sharper ranking so truncation cuts only weak passages
Skip building context for questions already answered
Let the model fetch more context itself when one pass is not enough

breaks.d: The key passage sits in the middle of a long context and is overlooked.
breaks.see: Answers ignore evidence that was in the prompt; accuracy drops as k grows
breaks.fix: Fewer passages, best ones at the start or end, rerank before packing

breaks.d: History plus passages exceed the window or squeeze the answer.
breaks.see: Token-limit errors or answers cut off mid-sentence
breaks.fix: Count tokens up front, reserve output room, compact old turns

breaks.d: Copies of one page fill most of the budget.
breaks.see: Many passages from the same URL; low source variety
breaks.fix: Near-duplicate removal and a per-source cap

breaks.d: A timestamp or per-user detail sits early in the prompt.
breaks.see: Cache read tokens near zero on repeated calls
breaks.fix: Move changing parts after the stable prefix

breaks.d: Passages have no date or source, so the model mixes old and new.
breaks.see: Answers quoting outdated numbers; citations hard to map
breaks.fix: Add id, title, URL and date to every passage

say: After reranking, my context builder packs the top passages into a fixed token budget, keeping room for instructions and the answer.
I dedupe near-identical chunks, expand winning chunks to their surrounding section, and label each with an id, URL and date so the model can cite it.
Because of the lost-in-the-middle effect, I keep the passage count small and place the strongest evidence at the start of the context.
I order the prompt with stable parts first so prompt caching reuses them, and for long agent runs I rely on compaction rather than an ever-growing history.

followups.q: With a 1M-token window, why not send everything?
followups.a: Cost and latency grow with every token, and models use long contexts unevenly - evidence in the middle gets missed. A tight, well-ranked context usually answers better and cheaper.
Empirically: run the eval set at several k values and plot answer correctness, citation recall and cost. Stop where quality flattens. Reranking lets you keep k small.

followups.q: How does ordering interact with prompt caching?
followups.a: Claude caches the prefix in the order tools, system, messages. Any change invalidates that level and everything after, so put stable content first and per-request content last.

followups.q: What about very long agent sessions?
followups.a: Use server-side compaction to summarise earlier turns and context editing to clear old tool results, so the agent keeps going without overflowing the window.

today: Current Claude Opus and Sonnet models default to a 1M-token window, and Anthropic names server-side compaction as the main way to manage context in long agent runs.

check.q: Where do models tend to use evidence worst in a long context?
check.why: The Lost in the Middle paper found a U-shape: start and end are used best.

check.q: Your budget is tight. What do you cut first?
check.why: Packing is ranking plus truncation - weak evidence goes first.

check.q: Prompt cache hits fell to zero after a change. Likely cause?
check.a: Something that changes each call moved into the prefix
check.why: Changes invalidate that level and everything after it.

check.q: Why expand a matched chunk to its neighbours?
check.a: Small chunks match well but carry too little context
check.why: Match small, read big: the model needs the surrounding thought.

sources.t: Liu et al. 2023: Lost in the Middle
